data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Heading
data.value: Executive Summary

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Problem_Heading
data.value: The Problem

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Problem_P1
data.value: AI governance programs are typically scoped to the outputs of systems that were already built, by processes governance had no role in, encoding assumptions governance was never positioned to examine.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Problem_P2
data.value: The decisions that determine what an AI system learns, what it is trained to recognize, what it is optimized to produce, and whose existence its training data was built to see clearly: these decisions are made at the training and fine-tuning layers, before the model exists. By the time a governance program is in place, those decisions are infrastructure. They cannot be undone by auditing outputs or documenting deployment decisions.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Problem_P3
data.value: This scope gap — governance defined as the management of consequences rather than the authorization of decisions — is what the Upstream Governance Framework addresses.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_ThreeLayerModel_Heading
data.value: The Three-Layer Model

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_ThreeLayerModel_Intro
data.value: The framework organizes upstream governance across three layers where consequential AI decisions are made:

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_ThreeLayerModel_Training
data.value: The training layer is where a model acquires its understanding of the world. Dataset curation, category design, optimization objectives, and representational review are governance decisions made here. For organizations deploying vendor models, this layer is controlled by the vendor. The framework defines what organizations can require vendors to disclose and be accountable for.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_ThreeLayerModel_FineTuning
data.value: The fine-tuning layer encompasses every decision an organization makes about how a vendor base model is configured, adapted, or extended for organizational use. It includes proprietary data selection, behavioral configuration, retrieval setup, and any mechanism that shapes model behavior. These are governance decisions.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_ThreeLayerModel_Deployment
data.value: The deployment layer is where the organization decides which AI system to deploy, for what purposes, and under what conditions. Vendor selection, use case authorization, and deployment scoping are governance decisions made here. For organizations that do not train or fine-tune their own models, this is where upstream governance begins.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_ThreeLayerModel_Outro
data.value: The framework does not replace deployment-layer governance programs or existing standards. It governs the layer those programs assume someone else already handled.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Components_Heading
data.value: What the Framework Contains

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Components_Intro
data.value: The framework consists of four components:

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Components_Item1
data.value: The Three-Layer Domain Model defines the governance domains present at each layer, the specific decisions that constitute governance decisions within each domain, the structural controls required, and the indicators that governance is absent.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Components_Item2
data.value: The Vendor Transparency Standards define what organizations have the right to require of vendors at selection and throughout the vendor relationship. They operationalize the governance obligation that exists at the deployment layer for organizations that cannot directly access vendor training decisions. They do not require vendors to provide direct access to training data. They require vendors to disclose what they can disclose and accept accountability for what they cannot.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Components_Item3
data.value: The Fine-Tuning Governance Protocol defines what organizations must govern when using proprietary data for fine-tuning. It covers data provenance requirements, consent documentation standards, category review process, and ongoing audit requirements.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Components_Item4
data.value: The Maturity Assessment Rubric is the diagnostic instrument that translates the framework into an organizational assessment. It scores governance maturity across all twelve domains in the three-layer model, produces a layer-by-layer maturity profile, and identifies the highest-priority governance gaps.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Standards_Heading
data.value: How This Framework Relates to Existing Standards

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Standards_NIST
data.value: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework operates primarily at the deployment and output layers. The upstream governance framework operates at the layer prior to where NIST AI RMF engages. The two frameworks are compatible and complementary.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Standards_EU
data.value: The EU AI Act's technical documentation requirements for high-risk systems include training data governance and bias assessment requirements at the training and fine-tuning layers. The upstream governance framework provides the governance architecture from which compliant documentation is produced.

data.name: ExecutiveSummary_Standards_ISO
data.value: ISO 42001 establishes AI management system requirements at the organizational level. The upstream governance framework specifies the operational content that an ISO 42001 management system must cover at the upstream layer.

data.name: Introduction_Heading
data.value: Framework Introduction

data.name: Introduction_Scope_Heading
data.value: Scope

data.name: Introduction_Scope_P1
data.value: The Upstream Governance Framework defines governance as the structural authorization of decisions before they are made, at the point where they can still be changed.

data.name: Introduction_Scope_P2
data.value: This framework governs the decisions that precede model deployment. It does not govern incident response, model monitoring, or output auditing. This framework is designed to operate prior to those functions, not instead of them.

data.name: Introduction_Scope_P3
data.value: This framework does not require organizations to access vendor training data. The vendor transparency standards defined in this framework require vendors to disclose what they can disclose and to accept accountability for what they cannot. The governance obligation the organization carries is to require that accountability, not to perform the vendor's governance for them.

data.name: Introduction_Scope_P4
data.value: This framework does not replace NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act, or ISO 42001. It operates at the layer those frameworks assume has already been governed.

data.name: Introduction_Usage_Heading
data.value: How to Use This Framework

data.name: Introduction_Usage_P1
data.value: The framework is organized in four parts. The Three-Layer Domain Model defines the governance domains, governance decisions, required structural controls, and absence indicators at each of the three layers. This is the specification against which an organization's governance program is measured.

data.name: Introduction_Usage_P2
data.value: The Vendor Transparency Standards define what to require of vendors at selection and throughout the relationship. The Fine-Tuning Governance Protocol defines what to govern when using proprietary data for fine-tuning.

data.name: Introduction_Usage_P3
data.value: The Maturity Assessment Rubric scores governance maturity across all twelve domains and identifies priority governance gaps.

data.name: Introduction_Usage_P4
data.value: The Standards Mapping section defines the standards mapping, licensing, and versioning terms.

data.name: Introduction_Usage_P5
data.value: Supporting documents are provided in three appendices: Appendix A contains field guidance for the Data Provenance Record, Appendix B contains field guidance for the Consent Documentation Record, and Appendix C contains relevant definitions. The Data Provenance Record, Consent Documentation Record, and Residual Risk Acceptance Record forms are available as standalone documents at kindredlabsfoundation.org.

data.name: Introduction_Conventions_Heading
data.value: Conventions

data.name: Introduction_Conventions_Intro
data.value: The following terms carry defined meanings throughout this document:

data.name: Introduction_Conventions_Must
data.value: Must denotes a binding requirement. An organization implementing this framework is required to meet every "must" statement.

data.name: Introduction_Conventions_Should
data.value: Should denotes a recommended practice. Departure from a "should" statement is permitted where the organization documents its reasoning.

data.name: Introduction_Conventions_May
data.value: May denotes a permitted option. No preference or requirement is implied.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Heading
data.value: Vendor Transparency Standards

data.name: VendorTransparency_Purpose_Heading
data.value: Purpose

data.name: VendorTransparency_Purpose_P1
data.value: The Vendor Transparency Standards define what organizations deploying vendor AI systems have the right to require, what vendors are obligated to disclose, and what accountability structures must exist as conditions of the vendor relationship. These standards operationalize the governance obligation that exists at the deployment layer for organizations that do not control the training layer directly.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Purpose_P2
data.value: The standards are organized into four components: disclosure requirements at selection, ongoing transparency obligations, contractual accountability structures, and vendor evaluation criteria.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Purpose_P3
data.value: These standards do not require vendors to provide direct access to training data. They require vendors to disclose what they can disclose and accept accountability for what they cannot.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_Heading
data.value: Disclosure Requirements at Selection

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_Intro
data.value: Before an organization selects a vendor AI system for deployment, the vendor must provide documentation sufficient for the organization's governance function to assess what upstream decisions have been made and what their governance implications are. The organization cannot authorize use cases for a system whose upstream decisions it cannot characterize.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_1_Heading
data.value: 1.1 Training Data Documentation

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_1_Content
data.value: The vendor must provide a written description of the training corpus including: the categories of data sources used, the date range of training data, the geographic and demographic scope of the data, and the criteria used to include or exclude data sources. The description need not identify proprietary sources but must be sufficient for the organization to assess representational scope.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_2_Heading
data.value: 1.2 Known Limitations and Bias Findings

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_2_Content
data.value: The vendor must disclose all known limitations of the system including published and internal bias evaluation findings, populations or use cases for which the system has demonstrated reduced accuracy or reliability, and any use cases the vendor explicitly does not recommend. This disclosure must include findings from third-party audits where they exist.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_3_Heading
data.value: 1.3 Optimization Objectives

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_3_Content
data.value: The vendor must describe what the system was optimized to produce, what trade-offs were made between competing objectives during training, and what the system treats as a correct output. This description must be sufficient for the organization to evaluate whether the optimization objective is appropriate for its intended use cases.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_4_Heading
data.value: 1.4 Category Architecture

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_4_Content
data.value: The vendor must disclose what categories the system is trained to recognize, classify, or predict, and must identify any categories that were treated as fixed during training. Where categories involve human characteristics, behaviors, or identities, the vendor must describe the basis on which those categories were defined.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_5_Heading
data.value: 1.5 Governance Documentation

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_5_Content
data.value: The vendor must provide documentation of its own internal governance process for the system being deployed, including:

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_5_Item1
data.value: what review process governed training data selection,

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_5_Item2
data.value: what authority existed to challenge or halt training,

data.name: VendorTransparency_Selection_1_5_Item3
data.value: and whether any independent review of the system's training was conducted.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Ongoing_Heading
data.value: Ongoing Transparency Obligations

data.name: VendorTransparency_Ongoing_Intro
data.value: The assumptions the organization relies on when it authorizes use cases are based on the system as it existed at selection. When the vendor changes the system materially, the organization's governance assessments may no longer be valid. Ongoing transparency obligations ensure the organization is informed when material changes occur.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Ongoing_2_1_Heading
data.value: 2.1 Material Model Updates

data.name: VendorTransparency_Ongoing_2_1_Content
data.value: The vendor must notify the organization in advance of any model update that materially alters the system's behavior, category architecture, optimization objectives, or known limitations. Notification must occur before the update is deployed to the organization's instance and must include sufficient description for the organization to assess whether its existing use case authorizations remain valid.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Ongoing_2_2_Heading
data.value: 2.2 New Bias or Limitation Findings

data.name: VendorTransparency_Ongoing_2_2_Content
data.value: The vendor must disclose any new bias evaluation findings, limitation discoveries, or third-party audit results that affect the system the organization is deploying, within a defined period of the vendor becoming aware of them. The organization's governance function must be notified directly, not through general product release notes.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Ongoing_2_3_Heading
data.value: 2.3 Training Data Changes

data.name: VendorTransparency_Ongoing_2_3_Content
data.value: Where the vendor retrains or significantly updates the model's training corpus, the vendor must disclose the nature of the change and its governance implications. The organization must be given sufficient time and information to update its base model assumption register before the retrained model is deployed.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Ongoing_2_4_Heading
data.value: 2.4 Incident Disclosure

data.name: VendorTransparency_Ongoing_2_4_Content
data.value: The vendor must disclose any material incident involving the system that the organization is deploying, including incidents at other client organizations where the failure mode is relevant to the organization's use cases. Incident disclosure must include the vendor's assessment of whether the incident originated in a training layer decision.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Contractual_Heading
data.value: Contractual Accountability Structures

data.name: VendorTransparency_Contractual_Intro
data.value: The following contractual provisions give the disclosure requirements structural force. They define consequences for non-disclosure, assign responsibility for training layer failures, and create an escalation path from deployment failures to vendor accountability.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Contractual_3_1_Heading
data.value: 3.1 Training Layer Responsibility

data.name: VendorTransparency_Contractual_3_1_Content
data.value: The vendor must accept contractual responsibility for failures that originate in training decisions the vendor made. This responsibility does not transfer to the organization simply because the organization deployed the system. The contract must define a process for determining whether a deployment failure has a training layer cause and must assign the vendor responsibility for remediation where training layer causation is established.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Contractual_3_2_Heading
data.value: 3.2 Disclosure Breach Remedy

data.name: VendorTransparency_Contractual_3_2_Content
data.value: The contract must define a specific remedy for the vendor's failure to make required disclosures, including failure to disclose known limitations at selection, failure to notify of material model updates, and failure to disclose new bias findings. The remedy must be sufficient to incentivize compliance, not merely acknowledge the breach.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Contractual_3_3_Heading
data.value: 3.3 Audit Rights

data.name: VendorTransparency_Contractual_3_3_Content
data.value: The organization must retain the right to commission an independent third-party audit of the vendor system at defined intervals or upon defined triggers. The vendor must cooperate with such audits within defined scope and timeframe. Audit rights must survive contract renewal and must not be conditioned on additional fees beyond reasonable scope costs.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Contractual_3_4_Heading
data.value: 3.4 Upstream Escalation Process

data.name: VendorTransparency_Contractual_3_4_Content
data.value: The contract must define a formal escalation process by which the organization can require the vendor to investigate whether a deployment failure originates in a training layer decision. The vendor must respond within a defined timeframe, must conduct the investigation at its own cost where training layer causation is plausible, and must provide the organization with findings sufficient to update its governance documentation.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Contractual_3_5_Heading
data.value: 3.5 Governance Representation

data.name: VendorTransparency_Contractual_3_5_Content
data.value: The vendor must represent that the disclosures made at selection are accurate and complete to the best of the vendor's knowledge, that no material information relevant to the organization's governance assessment has been withheld, and that the vendor's internal governance process for the system is as described. Misrepresentation of these matters must constitute a material breach.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_Heading
data.value: Vendor Evaluation Criteria

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_Intro
data.value: The vendor governance scorecard is the instrument organizations use to apply these standards at the selection stage. It translates the disclosure requirements and accountability structures into an evaluation framework the governance function applies during vendor selection.

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_Outro
data.value: The scorecard evaluates vendors across four dimensions:

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_1_Heading
data.value: 4.1 Disclosure Quality

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_1_Content
data.value: Does the vendor's documentation for each required disclosure provide sufficient information for a governance assessment, or does it satisfy the form of disclosure without the substance?

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_1_Criteria_Intro
data.value: Evaluation criteria:

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_1_Criteria_Item1
data.value: Completeness of training data description

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_1_Criteria_Item2
data.value: Specificity of known limitations disclosure

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_1_Criteria_Item3
data.value: Adequacy of optimization objective description

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_1_Criteria_Item4
data.value: Granularity of category architecture disclosure

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_1_Criteria_Item5
data.value: Evidence of internal governance process

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_2_Heading
data.value: 4.2 Governance Process Evidence

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_2_Content
data.value: Does the vendor provide credible evidence that upstream governance decisions were made through a structured process?

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_2_Criteria_Intro
data.value: Evaluation criteria:

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_2_Criteria_Item1
data.value: Evidence of pre-training review process

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_2_Criteria_Item2
data.value: Existence of third-party audit findings

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_2_Criteria_Item3
data.value: Structured bias evaluation methodology

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_2_Criteria_Item4
data.value: Named governance authority for training decisions

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_3_Heading
data.value: 4.3 Accountability Acceptance

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_3_Content
data.value: Is the vendor willing to accept the contractual accountability structures required by these standards?

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_3_Criteria_Intro
data.value: Evaluation criteria:

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_3_Criteria_Item1
data.value: Willingness to accept training layer responsibility provision

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_3_Criteria_Item2
data.value: Willingness to define disclosure breach remedy

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_3_Criteria_Item3
data.value: Acceptance of audit rights

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_3_Criteria_Item4
data.value: Willingness to define upstream escalation process

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_4_Heading
data.value: 4.4 Ongoing Transparency Track Record

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_4_Content
data.value: For vendors with existing deployments, what is the vendor's track record on ongoing transparency obligations?

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_4_Criteria_Intro
data.value: Evaluation criteria:

data.name: VendorTransparency_Evaluation_4_4_Criteria_Item1

data.name: DomainModel_Heading
data.value: Three-Layer Domain Model

data.name: DomainModel_Intro_P1
data.value: The domain model defines what governance means at each of the three layers where consequential AI decisions are made. All subsequent components are built against the specifications established here.

data.name: DomainModel_Intro_P2
data.value: For each of the three governance layers, this part defines the governance domains present at that layer, the specific decisions that constitute governance decisions within each domain, the structural controls required, and the indicators that governance is absent.

data.name: DomainModel_Intro_P3
data.value: A doctrinal governance program expresses values and principles without creating mechanisms to enforce them. A structural governance program creates named authority, formal process, documentation requirements, and defined consequences for non-compliance. This framework requires structural governance at every layer.

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Heading
data.value: Training

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Definition_Heading
data.value: Definition

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Definition_Content
data.value: The training layer encompasses every decision made about what data a model learns from, what it is trained to recognize or predict, and how its learning process is structured. Governance at this layer precedes the model's existence and cannot be retroactively applied.

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domains_Heading
data.value: Governance Domains

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain1_Heading
data.value: Domain 1.1: Dataset Curation

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain1_Content
data.value: The decisions governing what data enters the training corpus. Includes source selection, inclusion and exclusion criteria, data cleaning and filtering decisions, and the handling of gaps in representation.

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain1_Decisions_Intro
data.value: Governance decisions at this domain:

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain1_Decisions_Item1
data.value: What sources are eligible for inclusion and on what basis

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain1_Decisions_Item2
data.value: What criteria determine whether a data source is representative

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain1_Decisions_Item3
data.value: Who reviews inclusion and exclusion decisions and with what authority

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain1_Decisions_Item4
data.value: What consent basis is required for data about identifiable populations

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain1_Decisions_Item5
data.value: What representational gaps are acceptable and who decides acceptability

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain1_Decisions_Item6
data.value: How data cleaning decisions are documented and reviewed

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain2_Heading
data.value: Domain 1.2: Category Design

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain2_Content
data.value: The decisions governing what the system is trained to recognize, classify, or predict. Category design decisions determine what distinctions the model learns to make, what outcomes it learns to predict, and what boundaries it treats as fixed. These are governance decisions with consequences for every population the system subsequently affects.

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain2_Decisions_Intro
data.value: Governance decisions at this domain:

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain2_Decisions_Item1
data.value: What categories the training process treats as fixed versus contextual

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain2_Decisions_Item2
data.value: Who has authority to define or challenge category boundaries

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain2_Decisions_Item3
data.value: What review process exists before categories are encoded

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain2_Decisions_Item4
data.value: How contested or politically significant categories are handled

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain2_Decisions_Item5
data.value: What happens when a category boundary produces discriminatory outcomes

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain2_Decisions_Item6
data.value: How category decisions are documented for future audit

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain3_Heading
data.value: Domain 1.3: Training Architecture

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain3_Content
data.value: The decisions governing how the system learns: what it optimizes for, what it is penalized for, and what trade-offs are built into the learning process. Governance at this domain requires that optimization objectives are stated, justified, and reviewed before training begins.

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain3_Decisions_Intro
data.value: Governance decisions at this domain:

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain3_Decisions_Item1
data.value: What the model is optimized to produce and who authorized that objective

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain3_Decisions_Item2
data.value: What trade-offs between accuracy, fairness, and performance are acceptable

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain3_Decisions_Item3
data.value: Who reviews the optimization objective before training begins

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain3_Decisions_Item4
data.value: How changes to training objectives are authorized and documented

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain3_Decisions_Item5
data.value: What evaluation criteria determine whether training is complete

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain3_Decisions_Item6
data.value: Who has authority to halt or restart training based on evaluation results

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain4_Heading
data.value: Domain 1.4: Representational Review

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain4_Content
data.value: The structured process by which the training corpus and category design are evaluated for representational adequacy before training proceeds. Representational review requires named authority to assess, before training begins, which populations the training data represents adequately and which it does not.

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain4_Decisions_Intro
data.value: Governance decisions at this domain:

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain4_Decisions_Item1
data.value: Who conducts representational review and what authority they hold

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain4_Decisions_Item2
data.value: What populations or communities require explicit representation assessment

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain4_Decisions_Item3
data.value: What standard determines adequate representation

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain4_Decisions_Item4
data.value: What remediation is required when representation is inadequate

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain4_Decisions_Item5
data.value: Whether review findings can halt training and under what conditions

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Domain4_Decisions_Item6
data.value: How review findings are documented and retained

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Controls_Heading
data.value: Required Structural Controls

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Controls_Intro
data.value: For governance at this layer to be structural rather than doctrinal, the following controls must exist as formal processes with named authority, documentation requirements, and defined consequences for non-compliance:

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Controls_Item1
data.value: A pre-training review gate: no training proceeds without documented sign-off across all four domains

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Controls_Item2
data.value: Named authority for each domain: a specific role or body with defined scope and enforcement power

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Controls_Item3
data.value: A dataset provenance record: documentation of source, consent basis, and representational assessment for every dataset

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Controls_Item4
data.value: A category decision record: documentation of every category definition decision, rationale, and approving authority

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Controls_Item5
data.value: A training objective authorization: formal sign-off on optimization objectives before training begins, accompanied by a trade-off analysis documenting what was deprioritized between competing objectives and the governance basis for that decision

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Controls_Item6
data.value: A representational review report: findings, the specific standard or criteria applied to determine adequacy, remediation taken, and residual gaps acknowledged before training proceeds

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Indicators_Heading
data.value: Absence of Governance Indicators

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Indicators_Intro
data.value: An organization is ungoverned at this layer when:

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Indicators_Item1
data.value: Training data is selected by the technical team without a formal review process

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Indicators_Item2
data.value: Category boundaries are defined by model architects without governance involvement

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Indicators_Item3
data.value: Optimization objectives are set by product or technical leadership without documented review

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Indicators_Item4
data.value: No named authority exists for representational adequacy

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Indicators_Item5
data.value: Dataset provenance is tracked for legal compliance only, not governance

data.name: DomainModel_Training_Indicators_Item6
data.value: No pre-training gate exists: training proceeds without documented governance sign-off

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Heading
data.value: Fine-Tuning

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Definition_Heading
data.value: Definition

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Definition_P1
data.value: The fine-tuning layer encompasses every decision an organization makes about how a vendor base model is configured, adapted, or extended for organizational use. It includes decisions about what proprietary data the model learns from, what behavioral changes the organization is introducing, how retrieval is configured, and how any mechanism that shapes model behavior is designed and authorized. These are governance decisions.

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Definition_P2
data.value: Fine-tuning governance has two distinct upstream moments: what assumptions the vendor's base model already carries into the fine-tuning process, and what the organization's own configuration decisions are adding to or reinforcing in those assumptions. Both require governance.

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Definition_P3
data.value: The fine-tuning layer as defined here extends beyond model weight modification. Prompt engineering applied systematically at scale, agent tool configuration, memory system design, and policy classifiers each shape model behavior in ways that carry the same governance obligations as direct fine-tuning. Any mechanism through which an organization configures how the model behaves falls within this layer's scope.

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Domain2_Decisions_Item1
data.value: What the fine-tuning is designed to change in the model's behavior and who authorized that objective

That difference is entirely the organization's governance responsibility.

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Domain3_Decisions_Intro

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Controls_Item1
data.value: A pre-fine-tuning review gate: no fine-tuning begins without documented review across all four domains

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Controls_Item2

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Controls_Item3

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Controls_Item4

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Controls_Item5

A material change — defined as any addition or removal of source categories, change to retrieval weighting logic, or modification of authorization scope — requires a new governance review before the change is deployed

data.name: DomainModel_FineTuning_Controls_Item7

data.value: Definition

data.name: DomainModel_Deployment_Definition_Content
data.value: The deployment layer encompasses the decisions an organization makes about which AI system to deploy, for what purposes, and under what conditions. It includes vendor selection, use case authorization, deployment scoping, and accountability boundary definition. For organizations that do not train or fine-tune their own models, this is where upstream governance begins.

data.name: DomainModel_Deployment_Domains_Heading
data.value: Governance Domains

data.value: Domain 3.1: Vendor Selection

data.value: The decisions governing which AI system the organization adopts. Vendor selection determines what assumptions, training data, category design, and optimization objectives arrive pre-encoded in the system the organization will deploy. Governance evaluation of vendors includes what the system was built to optimize for, what its training data was designed to represent, and what structural accountability the vendor accepts for its upstream decisions.

data.value: Governance decisions at this domain:

data.name: DomainModel_Deployment_Domain1_Decisions_Item1

data.value: Who in the governance function has a formal role in vendor selection decisions

data.name: DomainModel_Deployment_Domain1_Decisions_Item4

data.name: DomainModel_Deployment_Domain1_Decisions_Item5

data.name: DomainModel_Deployment_Domain1_Decisions_Item6

Use case authorization defines what the system is and is not permitted to do, what populations it is authorized to affect, and what process governs the expansion of authorized use over time.

data.name: DomainModel_Deployment_Domain2_Decisions_Item1
data.value: What process exists to formally authorize each use case before deployment

data.value: Who has authority to authorize a use case and what criteria they apply

data.name: DomainModel_Deployment_Domain2_Decisions_Item5
data.value: How use case creep is monitored and brought back into the authorization process

data.name: DomainModel_Deployment_Domain2_Decisions_Item6

Deployment scoping defines the operational envelope of the system. Governance at this domain requires that the envelope is explicitly defined and reviewed on a regular cycle.

data.name: DomainModel_Deployment_Domain3_Decisions_Item1

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Heading
data.value: Layer Integration

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Purpose_Heading
data.value: Purpose

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Purpose_Content
data.value: The three layers do not operate independently. Decisions made at the training layer create conditions that fine-tuning governance must account for. Decisions made at fine-tuning create conditions that deployment governance must account for. Vendor decisions made outside the organization's direct control create governance obligations the organization must fulfill anyway. This section defines the handoff points between layers, the vendor decision surface, and the temporal structure that governs when each layer must be governed relative to the others.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_Heading
data.value: Layer Handoff Points

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_TtoFT_Heading
data.value: Training to Fine-Tuning

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_TtoFT_P1
data.value: What the training layer encodes arrives at the fine-tuning layer as the base model's assumptions. This has two governance implications.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_TtoFT_P2
data.value: First, the fine-tuning governance program must account for what it is inheriting. The base model assumption register defined in Layer 2 is the mechanism for this. Before fine-tuning begins, the organization must document what it knows and does not know about the assumptions already encoded in the model it is adapting.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_TtoFT_P3
data.value: Second, fine-tuning can reinforce, correct, or compound training layer assumptions. A fine-tuning objective designed without assessment of base model assumptions may deepen a representational gap the organization did not introduce. The pre-fine-tuning review gate must include explicit assessment of base model assumptions relative to the proposed fine-tuning objective.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_TtoFT_Requirement
data.value: Handoff governance requirement: the base model assumption register must be completed and reviewed before any fine-tuning objective is authorized.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_FTtoD_Heading
data.value: Fine-Tuning to Deployment

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_FTtoD_P1
data.value: What the fine-tuning layer produces arrives at the deployment layer as the customized model the organization will deploy. The deployment governance program must have documented knowledge of what fine-tuning has been done and what it was designed to change before use case authorization proceeds.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_FTtoD_P2
data.value: The customization scope boundary document defined in Layer 2 is the primary handoff artifact. It must be available to the deployment governance function before use case authorization proceeds. The use case authorization process must include explicit assessment of whether the proposed use case is within the appropriate scope of the system's customized behavior.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_FTtoD_Requirement
data.value: Handoff governance requirement: the customization scope boundary document must be current and reviewed by the deployment governance function before use case authorization for any fine-tuned system.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_DtoU_Heading
data.value: Deployment Back to Upstream

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_DtoU_P1
data.value: The handoff does not only run forward. Deployment failures carry diagnostic information about upstream decisions. A system that produces discriminatory outputs in production may reflect assumptions encoded at the training or fine-tuning layer. The framework requires a defined escalation path from deployment failure back to upstream review.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_DtoU_P2
data.value: The failure escalation protocol defined in Layer 3 is the mechanism. It must define specific triggers that move investigation from deployment governance to fine-tuning governance or training governance.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Handoffs_DtoU_Requirement
data.value: Handoff governance requirement: every deployment failure investigation must include an explicit determination of whether the failure signals a fine-tuning or training layer assumption. That determination must be documented regardless of whether escalation follows.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_VendorSurface_Heading
data.value: Vendor Decision Surface

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_VendorSurface_P1
data.value: Organizations deploying vendor models do not control the training layer directly. This creates a governance obligation that operates differently from the internal governance obligations defined in Layers 1 and 2.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_VendorSurface_P2
data.value: The vendor decision surface is the set of upstream decisions the vendor has made that shape the behavior of the system the organization deploys. It includes what the model was trained on, what categories it was trained to recognize, what it was optimized to produce, and what representational gaps exist in its training data.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_VendorSurface_P3
data.value: The organization cannot govern these decisions directly. It can require the vendor to be accountable for them. That accountability operates through three mechanisms:

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_VendorSurface_Mechanism1
data.value: Disclosure requirements at selection: the vendor must provide documentation of training data sources, known limitations, bias evaluation findings, and optimization objectives as a condition of selection. This is the vendor governance scorecard defined in Layer 3.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_VendorSurface_Mechanism2
data.value: Contractual accountability: the vendor must accept defined responsibility for failures that originate in training decisions, including a defined process for investigating whether a deployment failure has a training layer cause.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_VendorSurface_Mechanism3
data.value: Ongoing transparency obligations: the vendor must disclose material changes to the model that affect the assumptions the organization relied on at selection. Model updates that alter category behavior, representational characteristics, or optimization objectives are governance events requiring organizational review.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_VendorSurface_P4
data.value: Where a vendor declines to meet one or more of the disclosure or accountability requirements defined the Vendor Transparency Standards, the organization must not proceed as though the requirement does not apply. The governance function must produce a Residual Risk Acceptance Record documenting which requirements the vendor declined, what governance risk that creates, and the named authority's affirmative decision to proceed despite that risk. Proceeding without a completed Residual Risk Acceptance Record is a governance failure at Domain 3.1.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_VendorSurface_P5
data.value: The Vendor Transparency Standards operationalize these three mechanisms into contract language and procurement requirements.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_VendorSurface_P6
data.value: The Residual Risk Acceptance Record is available as a standalone form at kindredlabsfoundation.org. The record must document: the specific Vendor Transparency Standards requirement the vendor declined, the governance risk the gap creates, any compensating controls the organization is implementing, and the named authority's affirmative sign-off on the decision to proceed. The record must be completed before deployment proceeds and retained as a governance record.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Temporal_Heading
data.value: Temporal Structure

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Temporal_P1
data.value: Upstream governance is defined by its temporal logic. The decisions that require governance must be governed before the next layer begins.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Temporal_Intro
data.value: The required temporal sequence is:

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Temporal_Item1
data.value: Training layer governance must be complete before training begins. Dataset curation reviewed, categories approved, optimization objectives authorized, representational review completed and documented. If any of these are incomplete, training does not proceed.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Temporal_Item2
data.value: Fine-tuning layer governance must be complete before fine-tuning begins. Base model assumptions registered, proprietary data reviewed, fine-tuning objectives authorized, customization scope defined. The customization scope boundary document must reflect the current state of the model before fine-tuning adds to it.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Temporal_Item3
data.value: Deployment layer governance must be complete before deployment begins. Vendor governance scorecard completed, use cases authorized, deployment scope defined, accountability assignments documented, failure escalation protocol in place.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Temporal_P2
data.value: Each layer's governance completion is a formal gate with authority to stop what follows if requirements are not met. Post-deployment documentation does not satisfy the governance requirement.

data.name: DomainModel_Integration_Temporal_P3
data.value: The temporal structure also defines when governance re-engages after initial deployment. Fine-tuning changes require the fine-tuning governance process to run again before the updated model is deployed. Use case expansions require new use case authorization before the expansion goes live. Vendor model updates that materially change base model behavior require the base model assumption register to be updated before the updated model is deployed in production.

data.name: Protocol_Heading
data.value: Fine-Tuning Governance Protocol

data.name: Protocol_Purpose_Heading
data.value: Purpose

data.name: Protocol_Purpose_P1
data.value: The Fine-Tuning Governance Protocol defines what organizations must govern when they use proprietary data to fine-tune a vendor base model. It covers every organization that goes beyond deploying a vendor model as-is: those fine-tuning with employee data, customer data, behavioral data, operational data, or any other proprietary data source. It also covers organizations using retrieval-augmented generation at scale, where the retrieval corpus functions as a continuous fine-tuning mechanism.

data.name: Protocol_Purpose_P2
data.value: The underlying principle governing this protocol is that no data may be used to shape model behavior without documented provenance, consent basis, and governance review.

data.name: Protocol_Purpose_P3
data.value: The protocol is organized into four components: data provenance requirements, consent documentation standards, category review process, and ongoing audit requirements.

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_Heading
data.value: Data Provenance Requirements

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_Intro
data.value: Data provenance governance establishes where data came from, what it contains, and what it was originally collected for, before the organization determines whether it is appropriate for fine-tuning use. Provenance documentation is required for every dataset that enters the fine-tuning process. The governance question is not only whether the organization has the right to use the data, but whether using this data for this purpose is within the scope of authorized fine-tuning objectives.

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_Intro_Sub
data.value: See Appendix A: Data Provenance Record Template for the implementation form instructions for this component.

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_1_1_Heading
data.value: 1.1 Source Identification

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_1_1_Content
data.value: The origin of the dataset must be documented: what system, process, or activity generated it, what time period it covers, and what population it reflects. For data generated by organizational processes, the documentation must identify whether the process that generated the data was itself subject to bias or differential treatment that would be reproduced in the fine-tuning corpus.

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_1_2_Heading
data.value: 1.2 Original Collection Purpose

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_1_2_Content
data.value: The purpose for which the data was originally collected must be documented and assessed for compatibility with fine-tuning use. The provenance record must assess whether the individuals whose data this is had awareness that it might be used for AI model training.

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_1_3_Heading
data.value: 1.3 Representational Scope

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_1_3_Content
data.value: The provenance record must document what populations, behaviors, or conditions the data reflects and what it does not. A dataset generated by organizational processes reflects the organization's history, including historical patterns of access, opportunity, and treatment. Those patterns must be assessed as part of the provenance review.

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_1_4_Heading
data.value: 1.4 Known Data Quality Issues

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_1_4_Content
data.value: Any known quality issues must be documented: gaps, anomalies, periods of unreliable data collection, and conditions under which the data may not accurately reflect the population it purports to represent. The governance assessment must include whether known limitations would produce systematic misrepresentation when encoded through fine-tuning.

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_1_5_Heading
data.value: 1.5 Prior Use History

data.name: Protocol_DataProvenance_1_5_Content
data.value: Where the dataset has been used in prior fine-tuning or model development, that history must be documented. Cumulative fine-tuning on the same dataset can compound representational assumptions across model generations. The provenance record must reflect prior use history so the governance review can assess cumulative effect.

data.name: Protocol_Consent_Heading
data.value: Consent Documentation Standards

data.name: Protocol_Consent_Intro
data.value: Consent documentation establishes the basis on which the organization is authorized to use data about identifiable people for fine-tuning purposes. This is distinct from the legal question of whether the organization has terms of service that permit broad data use. The governance question is whether the people whose data is being used for fine-tuning were meaningfully informed that their data would be used for this purpose and whether they had a meaningful opportunity to object. Both the legal basis and the governance basis must be documented.

data.name: Protocol_Consent_Intro_Sub
data.value: See Appendix B: Consent Documentation Template for the implementation form instructions for this component.

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_1_Heading
data.value: 2.1 Consent Basis Classification

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_1_Intro
data.value: Every dataset entering fine-tuning must be classified by consent basis. Four classifications apply:

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_1_Explicit
data.value: Explicit consent: the individuals whose data is included were specifically informed that their data would be used for AI training or fine-tuning and affirmatively agreed.

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_1_Informed
data.value: Informed general consent: the individuals whose data is included were informed that their data might be used for purposes including AI development, in terms sufficiently specific that AI fine-tuning was a reasonably foreseeable use.

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_1_Implied
data.value: Implied organizational consent: the data was generated within an employment or service relationship where AI development use was disclosed as an organizational practice at the time the relationship was established.

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_1_NoBasis
data.value: No documented consent basis: the data is being used without a documented basis for the individuals' awareness of this use. This classification does not automatically prohibit use. It triggers elevated review. The governance function must make an affirmative decision that the use is appropriate despite the absence of a documented consent basis, and that decision must be recorded.

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_2_Heading
data.value: 2.2 Consent Basis Documentation

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_2_Intro
data.value: For each dataset, the documentation that establishes the consent basis must be identified and retained:

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_2_Item1
data.value: the specific terms of service language,

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_2_Item2
data.value: employment agreement provision,

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_2_Item3
data.value: privacy notice,

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_2_Item4
data.value: or other instrument that establishes the basis.

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_2_Outro
data.value: Where no such document exists, the absence must be recorded and the elevated review process initiated.

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_3_Heading
data.value: 2.3 Consent Scope Assessment

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_3_Content
data.value: The documented consent basis must be assessed against the specific fine-tuning use. The assessment must determine whether a reasonable person who provided this consent would understand it to cover this specific use.

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_4_Heading
data.value: 2.4 Withdrawal and Deletion Obligations

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_4_Intro
data.value: The consent documentation must address what happens when an individual withdraws consent or requests deletion of their data. The protocol must define:

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_4_Item1
data.value: whether withdrawal from the original data source requires removal from the fine-tuning corpus,

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_4_Item2
data.value: what the process is for removing data from a fine-tuning corpus that has already been used,

data.name: Protocol_Consent_2_4_Item3
data.value: and what the organization's obligation is to individuals whose data has already shaped a deployed model.

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_Heading
data.value: Category Review Process

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_Intro
data.value: Category review examines what the fine-tuning is teaching the model to recognize, distinguish, or predict. Fine-tuning objectives encode assumptions about what distinctions matter and how to make them. Category review is the governance process that ensures those assumptions are explicitly identified and authorized before fine-tuning begins.

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_1_Heading
data.value: 3.1 Category Inventory

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_1_Intro
data.value: Before fine-tuning begins, the governance function must produce an inventory of the categories the fine-tuning objective will reinforce or introduce. A category in this context is any distinction the model is being trained to make:

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_1_Item1
data.value: between high-performing and low-performing employees,

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_1_Item2
data.value: between high-risk and low-risk customers,

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_1_Item3
data.value: between qualified and unqualified applicants.

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_1_Outro
data.value: The inventory must name each category explicitly. Unnamed categories cannot be reviewed.

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_2_Heading
data.value: 3.2 Category Origin Assessment

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_2_Intro
data.value: For each category in the inventory, the review must assess where the category came from. Three origins require different governance treatment:

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_2_Origin1
data.value: Vendor-inherited categories: distinctions the base model already makes that the fine-tuning will reinforce. These require assessment of whether the vendor's category design is appropriate for the organization's use case and population.

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_2_Origin2
data.value: Data-derived categories: distinctions that emerge from patterns in the fine-tuning data rather than from explicit design. These require careful review because they may encode historical organizational patterns that were not part of the stated fine-tuning objective.

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_2_Origin3
data.value: Explicitly designed categories: distinctions the organization has deliberately chosen to build into the fine-tuning objective. These require the clearest governance rationale and the most explicit authorization.

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_3_Heading
data.value: 3.3 Contested Category Protocol

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_3_Intro
data.value: Any category that involves human characteristics, behaviors, identities, or assessments of human value or capability is a contested category and requires elevated review. The elevated review must include:

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_3_Item1
data.value: A named authority who approves the category's inclusion

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_3_Item2
data.value: A documented rationale for why the distinction is appropriate for the use case

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_3_Item3
data.value: An assessment of differential outcomes across protected or vulnerable populations

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_3_Item4
data.value: A defined review schedule for reassessment after deployment

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_4_Heading
data.value: 3.4 Category Authorization

data.name: Protocol_CategoryReview_3_4_Content
data.value: No fine-tuning may proceed until every category in the inventory has been reviewed and authorized by named governance authority. The authorization must be recorded: who authorized each category, on what basis, and what conditions or review requirements attach to the authorization. Category authorization is not permanent. It must be renewed when the fine-tuning objective changes, when the data corpus changes materially, or on the defined review schedule.

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_Heading
data.value: Ongoing Audit Requirements

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_Purpose_Heading
data.value: Purpose

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_Purpose_Content
data.value: Fine-tuning governance does not end when fine-tuning is complete. The model the fine-tuning produced continues to operate on the basis of what it learned. Ongoing audit requirements ensure the organization maintains visibility into what its fine-tuning decisions produced and retains the ability to identify when a correction is needed.

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_1_Heading
data.value: 4.1 Fine-Tuning Inventory

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_1_Content
data.value: The organization must maintain a current inventory of all fine-tuning that has been applied to models in active deployment. The inventory must include: what fine-tuning was applied, when, using what data, for what objective, under what authorization, and what version of the base model it was applied to. This inventory is the organizational record of what proprietary data has shaped what deployed models.

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_2_Heading
data.value: 4.2 Audit Cycle

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_2_Content
data.value: The fine-tuning data and category authorizations for each deployed model must be reviewed on a defined cycle, not to exceed twelve months. The review must assess: whether the data corpus remains representative of the population the model is currently serving, whether any new quality issues or bias findings have emerged, whether the consent basis for any data in the corpus has changed, and whether the category authorizations remain appropriate given how the model has performed in deployment.

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_3_Heading
data.value: 4.3 Out-of-Cycle Review Triggers

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_3_Intro
data.value: The following events must trigger an out-of-cycle review regardless of where the organization is in its audit schedule:

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_3_Item1
data.value: A deployment failure routed to the fine-tuning layer

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_3_Item2
data.value: A material change in the population the model is serving

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_3_Item3
data.value: A significant change in the organizational processes that generated the fine-tuning data

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_3_Item4
data.value: A legal or regulatory development affecting the consent basis for data in the corpus

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_3_Item5
data.value: A vendor finding regarding the base model that may interact with the organization's fine-tuning decisions

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_4_Heading
data.value: 4.4 Correction Protocol

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_4_Content
data.value: Where an audit identifies a fine-tuning governance failure, the correction protocol must define: what immediate steps are required to limit harm from the deployed model while correction is underway, what the process is for correcting the fine-tuning corpus or objective, what authority must authorize the corrected fine-tuning before it is deployed, and what documentation is required to close the governance finding.

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_5_Heading
data.value: 4.5 Sunset and Retirement

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_5_Intro
data.value: Fine-tuning applied to a model that is retired from deployment does not automatically cease to be a governance concern. The organization must document:

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_5_Item1
data.value: what happened to the fine-tuned model at retirement,

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_5_Item2
data.value: whether the fine-tuning corpus or any derivatives remain in organizational systems,

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_5_Item3
data.value: and whether any subsequently deployed model inherited assumptions from the retired model's fine-tuning.

data.name: Protocol_OngoingAudit_4_5_Outro
data.value: The governance record for retired models must be retained for a defined period.

data.name: Maturity_Heading
data.value: Maturity Assessment Rubric

data.name: Maturity_Purpose_Heading
data.value: Purpose

data.name: Maturity_Purpose_P1
data.value: The Maturity Assessment Rubric is the diagnostic instrument that translates the framework into an organizational assessment. It scores governance maturity across every domain defined in the Three-Layer Domain Model, identifies specific gaps, and produces a layer-by-layer maturity profile.

data.name: Maturity_Purpose_P2
data.value: The rubric is built against the absence of governance indicators defined in each layer, the structural controls required at each layer, and the handoff requirements defined in the Layer Integration section.

data.name: Maturity_Purpose_P3
data.value:
The rubric is designed for two uses:
  • self-assessment with facilitated guidance,
  • and governance architecture engagement.

data.name: Maturity_Purpose_P4
data.value: The questions are written to be legible to governance and compliance functions without requiring technical expertise to answer.

data.name: Maturity_Levels_Heading
data.value: Maturity Levels

data.name: Maturity_Levels_Level0_Heading
data.value: Level 0: Absent

data.name: Maturity_Levels_Level0_Content
data.value: No governance structure exists at this domain. The decisions within this domain are being made without any formal review, documentation, or named authority.

data.name: Maturity_Levels_Level1_Heading
data.value: Level 1: Nascent

data.name: Maturity_Levels_Level1_Content
data.value: Awareness of the governance need exists but no formal process or documentation has been established. Governance at this domain happens informally or inconsistently, dependent on individual judgment rather than organizational structure.

data.name: Maturity_Levels_Level2_Heading
data.value: Level 2: Developing

data.name: Maturity_Levels_Level2_Content
data.value: A formal process exists but is incomplete, inconsistently applied, or lacks one or more required structural elements. Documentation exists but may be incomplete. Named authority exists but may lack enforcement power. The governance structure is present in outline but not in full operation.

data.name: Maturity_Levels_Level3_Heading
data.value: Level 3: Structural

data.name: Maturity_Levels_Level3_Content
data.value: Governance is embedded in decision-making processes with named authority, complete documentation requirements, defined consequences for non-compliance, and a functioning review cycle. The governance structure operates independently of the individuals currently filling governance roles. It would survive personnel change.

data.name: Maturity_Scoring_Heading
data.value: Scoring Architecture

data.name: Maturity_Scoring_P1
data.value: Each domain is scored 0 through 3 against the maturity levels above. The score reflects the weakest structural element present, not an average. A domain with a defined process but no named authority scores 1, not 2, because the absence of named authority means the process cannot be enforced.

data.name: Maturity_Scoring_P2
data.value: Domains are grouped by layer. Layer scores are the average of domain scores within that layer, rounded down. The overall maturity profile is not a single aggregate score. It is a layer-by-layer profile that shows where governance is strongest and where the gaps are most consequential.

data.name: Maturity_Scoring_P3
data.value: Weighting note: Layer 1 (Training) and Layer 2 (Fine-Tuning) gaps carry greater governance consequence than Layer 3 (Deployment) gaps because they are less recoverable. A deployment decision can be reversed. A training decision that encoded a structural assumption into a deployed model cannot be undone without retraining. The rubric does not numerically weight by layer but the diagnostic narrative must reflect this asymmetry.

data.name: Maturity_Instrument_Heading
data.value: Assessment Instrument

data.name: Maturity_Instrument_Intro
data.value: The instrument is organized by layer and domain. For each domain, the assessor asks the following questions in order. The first question answered "no" determines the domain score. If all questions are answered "yes," the domain scores Level 3.

data.name: Maturity_Instrument_Training_Heading
data.value: Training

data.name: Maturity_Instrument_Training_Intro
data.value: Organizations that do not train their own models score Layer 1 domains against what they know or can require their vendor to disclose. The base model assumption register in Layer 2 is the mechanism for documenting vendor-dependent domain assessments.

data.name: Standards_Mapping_Heading
data.value: Standards Mapping

data.name: Standards_Mapping_Purpose_Heading
data.value: Purpose

data.name: Standards_Mapping_Purpose_Content
data.value: The standards mapping defines how the Upstream Governance Framework relates to existing AI governance standards. It identifies where the frameworks are complementary, where they overlap, and where they address distinct governance problems.

data.name: Standards_NIST_Heading
data.value: NIST AI Risk Management Framework

data.name: Standards_NIST_Content_P1
data.value: The NIST AI RMF organizes AI governance around four functions: Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. It is a risk management framework applied to AI. Its Govern function addresses organizational roles and responsibilities. Its Map function addresses AI system context and risk identification. Its Measure function addresses risk analysis and evaluation. Its Manage function addresses risk response and recovery.

data.name: Standards_NIST_Relationship
data.value: Relationship to the upstream governance framework: the NIST AI RMF operates primarily at the deployment layer and at the output layer. Its Map function touches the upstream layer in identifying AI system context but does not define governance requirements for the decisions that created that context. The upstream governance framework operates at the layer prior to where NIST AI RMF engages.

data.name: Standards_NIST_Compatibility
data.value: Compatibility: the upstream governance framework is designed to be compatible with NIST AI RMF. The governance records and documentation requirements defined in the upstream framework provide input to NIST AI RMF's Map and Measure functions. Organizations that are NIST AI RMF aligned can adopt the upstream governance framework without replacing or conflicting with their existing alignment.

data.name: Standards_EU_Heading
data.value: EU AI Act

data.name: Standards_EU_Content_P1
data.value: The EU AI Act establishes risk-based requirements for AI systems deployed in the European Union, with the most stringent requirements applying to high-risk AI systems. It requires conformity assessments, technical documentation, human oversight, transparency, and post-market monitoring for high-risk systems.

data.name: Standards_EU_Relationship
data.value: Relationship to the upstream governance framework: the EU AI Act's technical documentation requirements for high-risk systems include requirements for training data governance, data quality, and bias assessment. These requirements operate at the training layer and the fine-tuning layer. The upstream governance framework provides a structured governance architecture for meeting these requirements. Organizations subject to the EU AI Act that implement the upstream governance framework will have governance documentation that supports their Act compliance obligations.

data.name: Standards_EU_Compatibility
data.value: Compatibility: the upstream governance framework's documentation requirements for dataset provenance, category review, and training objective authorization directly support the EU AI Act's technical documentation requirements for high-risk systems. The framework does not replace Act compliance but provides the governance structure from which compliant documentation is produced.

data.name: Standards_ISO_Content_P1
data.value: ISO 42001 is the international standard for AI management systems. It follows the ISO management system structure familiar from ISO 9001 and ISO 27001: establishing context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, and improvement. It addresses AI governance at the organizational management system level.

data.name: Standards_ISO_Relationship
data.value: Relationship to the upstream governance framework: ISO 42001 establishes management system requirements for responsible AI development and use. It addresses governance at the policy and management system level rather than specifying governance requirements for particular upstream decisions. The upstream governance framework specifies what the governance decisions at each layer are and what structural controls are required. It operates at the decision and process level where ISO 42001 operates at the management system level.

data.name: Standards_ISO_Compatibility
data.value: Compatibility: the upstream governance framework is designed to operate within an ISO 42001 management system. The governance domains, structural controls, and documentation requirements defined in the upstream framework are the operational content that an ISO 42001 AI management system governs. Organizations implementing ISO 42001 can use the upstream governance framework to specify what their management system must cover at the upstream layer.
